title: StratoEdge capacity hardening & surge playtest intake
transcript_header: Date: 2025-11-06 | Start: 15:00 PST | Duration: 47m | Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/rec/placeholder | Attendees: Maya, Connor (Redwood) — Liam, Priya, Diego, Sara (StratoEdge)
summary: Discovery call to qualify StratoEdge's requirements for a Dedicated GPU deployment. Main concerns: tenant isolation, predictable burst handling, fallback to hosted models, and security (KMS/SOC2). Agreed pilot: Redwood to run a surge simulation with customer traces and follow up with pricing + a recommended topology (hot pool + prewarm strategy).
topics: Current traffic profile and pain points
Burst strategy: warm pool, pre-warm, and fallback
next_steps: Redwood to send tailored capacity proposal and pricing (incl. hot-pool options)
Connor to run simulated burst test using StratoEdge traces and share perf/cost numbers
StratoEdge to provide 2 weeks of traffic traces and p95/p99 latency targets
Schedule 60-min pilot kickoff (engineers only) w/in 2 weeks
action_items: Maya Chen - send pricing + reserved node T&Cs - due 2025-11-10
Connor Patel - run surge sim with StratoEdge traces and share results - due 2025-11-14
Priya Mehta - export 14 days of token and latency histograms and share - due 2025-11-09
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we can start in a minute. This is Maya from Redwood Inference, I'm the AE on the account. Connor from our SE team is here as well. 
[00:12] Liam O'Connor: Thanks Maya, hey team, Liam here. We just pulled people in — Priya, Diego and Sara are with me. 
[00:22] Connor Patel: Hey, quick intro — I focus on dedicated deployments and the runtime. Happy to dive into topology and bursting. 
[00:28] Priya Mehta: Hi all, Priya. We're running inference for a conversational analytics product — mostly shorter prompts but occasional long-run summarization jobs. We see spikes during end of day and enterprise batch runs. 
[00:39] Diego Ramos: Diego here, infra. Our current setup is multi-tenant k8s on AWS, GPUs are on-demand right now but cost is spiking during bursts. 
[00:48] Maya Chen: Great, high level: you told us you wanted predictable latency and cost during spikes and better isolation for enterprise customers — correct? 
[00:58] Liam O'Connor: Correct. We have some enterprise customers that require VPC isolation, and one health partner asking for on-prem options for a subset of workloads. 
[01:08] Connor Patel: Makes sense. Quick qualifier: what's your target p95 latency for interactive flows and what's acceptable for batch summarization? 
[01:16] Priya Mehta: For interactive we want p95 < 200ms ideally, p99 < 500ms. For the long summarizations, up to 4s is ok as long as throughput is predictable. 
[01:27] Maya Chen: OK. And current traffic shape — average RPS, token sizes, and how big are the spikes? 
[01:35] Priya Mehta: Average is about 12 RPS with median request size ~120 tokens, but we see spikes to ~300 RPS for 10-15 minutes during certain events. There's also nightly batch windows where a few hundred long requests run concurrently. 
[01:47] Connor Patel: Helpful. So two burst patterns: short high-frequency spikes and longer concurrent batches. That maps well to a hot-pool plus prewarm strategy we usually recommend. 
[01:57] Diego Ramos: When you say hot-pool, are we talking reserved nodes kept idle? We're worried about cost leakage if they sit idle. 
[02:06] Connor Patel: Right, small nuance. Hot-pool is a lightweight kept-warm pool with low-cost reserved capacity, not full-bore GPUs idle. For short spikes we can keep a small set of instances with warmed KV cache and minimal replicas to accept connections quickly. Then we can auto-scale into dedicated reserved nodes for sustained load. 
[02:22] Liam O'Connor: And what's the fallback if the reserved pool is exhausted? We can't have customer-facing errors. 
[02:28] Maya Chen: We typically recommend a graceful fallback chain: 1) auto-burst to compatible hosted variants (lower-memory/quantized), 2) route to regional fallback cluster, 3) queue with rate-limited retries if all else fails. You can set per-tenant fallback policies. 
[02:42] Priya Mehta: How disruptive is a hosted fallback for us? We need consistent outputs for certain customers. 
[02:48] Connor Patel: Hosted fallback can introduce small quality deltas if the hosted model is a different quant or size. For strict customers you can pin them to private/dedicated variants only — in which case we set preemption and throttling policies instead of fallback to hosted. That said, for most workloads we recommend a fallback to a compatible variant and flagging any regressions for rollback. 
[03:03] Diego Ramos: What about VPC integrations and KMS? We need keys to stay in our control for some PHI-related customers. 
[03:10] Maya Chen: Redwood Private supports a customer-managed control plane and VPC connectors; we also integrate with AWS KMS and HSMs for key storage, and can do a bring-your-own-KMS flow. We'll share our SOC2 plus the KMS integration doc. 
[03:24] Liam O'Connor: Good. Do you do any audit logging for token-level access? We need to show who called what model and at what time. 
[03:30] Connor Patel: Yes — we provide request-level audit logs, per-route tracing, and token/latency breakdowns in the Console. Logs can be exported to your SIEM or to S3 with enforced retention policies. 
[03:42] Priya Mehta: On the technical side — what GPU types do you support for Dedicated pools? We prefer A100s for large models but are open to quantized LLMs on cheaper T4-like hardware for embeddings. 
[03:53] Connor Patel: For Dedicated we support A100 and H100 families for large autoregressive work. We also have support for lower-cost options for quantized variants; the runtime will pick kernels appropriate to the quant format. We'll show you performance profiles for typical sequence lengths and the model catalog. 
[04:07] Sara Kim: Quick question on deployments: can we mix hosted and private? We want most traffic on hosted but enterprise customers on private. 
[04:14] Maya Chen: Absolutely — hybrid routing is common. You can target specific tenants to a Dedicated cluster (or Private) while using Hosted for general traffic, with routing policies and canaries. 
[04:24] Liam O'Connor: Cost targets — we're trying to keep token cost under $0.02 per 1k tokens for inference across the board. Do you have numbers for Dedicated idle and per-token costs? 
[04:35] Connor Patel: It varies with utilization and model. Dedicated unit economics improve with higher sustained utilization. For your spike patterns, the hot-pool + bursting into reserved nodes typically gets you close but we'll run the surge sim to give per-1k token estimates for your profile. 
[04:50] Priya Mehta: Can you walk us through the surge sim — what data do you need and what outputs will we get? 
[04:56] Connor Patel: We'll need 14 days of request traces: timestamp, token counts, model, and latency. We'll replay them against different topology configs (hot-pool sizes, reserved node counts, prewarm thresholds) and return p95/p99 latency, cost estimates, and expected fallback frequency. 
[05:11] Diego Ramos: Is that safe to share? We have redacted traces we can provide. 
[05:14] Maya Chen: Redacted traces are fine. We only need the traffic shape and token distributions. We'll treat them under our NDA if needed. 
[05:21] Liam O'Connor: On the isolation side, if a tenant needs full VPC or on-prem requirement, what's the onboarding process? 
[05:28] Connor Patel: Two paths: 1) Private deployment — we ship a customer-managed control plane and connectors so data never leaves your VPC; 2) On-prem package — for air-gapped you run our inference runtime in your environment; we provide support and hardened images. We'll need a security handoff for both (networking, firewall rules, KMS). 
[05:44] Priya Mehta: For the on-prem option, how do upgrades work? We need predictable maintenance windows. 
[05:49] Maya Chen: We coordinate upgrades with your SREs and can do canary rollouts. For Private/on-prem we document the upgrade path and can schedule maintenance windows that align with your batch windows. 
[05:58] Connor Patel: Quick note on quantization: we often recommend a mixed approach. Keep critical tenants on FP16 A100s, move tolerant workloads to int8/int4 quantized variants to save cost. The runtime handles kernel switchovers and KV cache compatibility but you'll want to validate outputs. 
[06:13] Priya Mehta: That matches our thinking. One more: preemption — if reserved nodes are shared and preemptable, what guarantees do we have? 
[06:20] Connor Patel: For Dedicated reserved nodes, preemption is configurable. You can have strict isolation (no preemption) for a higher commit price, or allow preemption with fast fallback for cost savings. We can map eviction policies to tenant SLAs. 
[06:33] Liam O'Connor: Any case studies of similar customers who had 10x spikes and we reduced cost? 
[06:38] Maya Chen: Yes — we have a case where a SaaS analytics customer paired hot-pools with prefix caching and reduced token costs by ~40% during spikes while maintaining p95. I'll send the short case study after the call. 
[06:50] Sara Kim: For the pilot — what minimum commitment do you expect? 
[06:54] Maya Chen: For the pilot we usually do a short-term reserved capacity trial (2-4 weeks) or a burst eval where we simulate spikes against hosted+Dedic combo. No long-term financial commitment until you decide to commit to Dedicated. 
[07:06] Priya Mehta: Ok. For SLOs — if p95 breaches happen during a spike, how do we get alerted? 
[07:12] Connor Patel: Console has alerting and traces; we can integrate with PagerDuty. We also emit metrics for token cost and fallback events so you can trigger alerts on fallback frequency. 
[07:22] Diego Ramos: Networking — do we need private links for VPC? 
[07:25] Connor Patel: Yes, we support PrivateLink and VPC peering for low-latency ingress. For on-prem, we do a secure VPN or direct connect if needed. 
[07:35] Liam O'Connor: Let's dig into a little scenario — if we get a sudden 8x RPS spike for 12 minutes, what's the recommended topology? 
[07:43] Connor Patel: Short answer: a small hot-pool sized to absorb the first 30-60s and fast autoscaler into reserved nodes with a prewarm threshold at 60% CPU/GPU util. Also tune batching windows and async queueing for tolerant requests. We'll simulate exact numbers with your traces. 
[07:58] Priya Mehta: Any pitfalls we should watch for? We've been bitten by cold starts and KV cache misses that cause token blowups. 
[08:05] Connor Patel: Right — KV cache warming is key. Using prefix caching for repeated context and keeping a small hot-pool with warmed KV state reduces cold-start overhead dramatically. Also watch batching: overbatching for short-interactive flows increases latency tail. 
[08:18] Maya Chen: Moving to security: SOC 2 is a checkbox for you? 
[08:22] Liam O'Connor: Yes, SOC 2 Type II is required for one of our large clients, plus SSO/SAML and RBAC controls. 
[08:30] Maya Chen: We have SOC2, SSO via SAML/OIDC, and role-based access. We'll include our compliance pack and the SSO setup doc. 
[08:38] Diego Ramos: Encryption at rest — do logs contain PII? We need redaction. 
[08:42] Connor Patel: We can configure request log redaction and limit retention. For PHI workloads, we'd push you toward Private/on-prem with customer-managed KMS. 
[08:53] Priya Mehta: About rollout — if we wanted to onboard 5 enterprise tenants to dedicated clusters first, what is the timeline? 
[08:59] Maya Chen: Typical ramp is 4-6 weeks from commitment: contract, network handoff, initial cluster provisioning, and a test pilot. Could be faster with prioritized SLA. 
[09:10] Liam O'Connor: Cost control question: can we enforce tenant quotas so one tenant can't exhaust the warm pool? 
[09:16] Connor Patel: Yes, per-tenant quotas and rate limits are configurable. You can set hard caps, token budgets, and fallback priority. 
[09:25] Sara Kim: Can we run A/B with quantized vs fp16 to validate quality? 
[09:28] Connor Patel: Absolutely. Redwood Optimize can run evals across prompt sets and flag regressions when switching quantization profiles. We can integrate your prompt sets into that pipeline. 
[09:40] Priya Mehta: Let's talk SLA numbers — what's your standard uptime and latency SLOs for Dedicated? 
[09:46] Maya Chen: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed uptime of 99.9% with latency targets tied to model profiles; exact terms vary by contract. We can provide a draft SLA with the proposal. 
[09:55] Liam O'Connor: On data residency — some customers must keep EU data in EU. Can routing be region-aware? 
[10:00] Connor Patel: Yes, routing by region is supported, with regional model variants and regional Dedicated clusters if needed. 
[10:09] Diego Ramos: Do you do synthetic load tests or chaos tests? 
[10:12] Connor Patel: We can run synthetic burst replays and also work with your infra team to run controlled chaos/failure injections. Part of the pilot can include a failover test. 
[10:22] Maya Chen: Okay, I'm going to propose a concrete pilot: we run a 2-week surge simulation plus a 48-hour live pilot with a small reserved hot-pool. Connor will run the replay, and then we'll run an optional live window where we route a shadow copy of traffic. 
[10:34] Priya Mehta: Sounds good. For replay, the outputs you return — p95/p99, cost delta, and fallback frequency — is that right? 
[10:39] Connor Patel: Yes, and a recommended topology matrix with predicted warm-pool size and reserved node counts. 
[10:45] Liam O'Connor: One more question — billing granularity, hourly or per-minute? 
[10:49] Maya Chen: Billing is typically per-hour for reserved capacity plus per-token for hosted workloads. We'll detail the calculation in the proposal. 
[10:58] Sara Kim: We'd also like to know about operational runbooks for failover. 
[11:03] Connor Patel: We have runbooks for preemptions, autoscaler behavior, and rollback. We'll share a sample runbook and playbook for burst scenarios. 
[11:13] Priya Mehta: Are there any known limitations for long KV-heavy generations? 
[11:17] Connor Patel: For very long sequences the memory profile changes; we recommend H100/A100 with larger memory footprints and monitoring for KV cache eviction. We can size nodes accordingly. 
[11:28] Diego Ramos: Do you support mixed tenancy topology where some tenants are pinned to physical GPUs? 
[11:33] Connor Patel: Yes, we support strict pinning with dedicated physical instances for ultra-sensitive tenants. That comes with higher cost but strong isolation. 
[11:42] Liam O'Connor: Let's surface a few acceptance criteria for the pilot: 1) interactive p95 < 250ms during 8x spike, 2) fallback events < 1% of requests, 3) cost delta < 30% vs current on-demand. 
[11:56] Maya Chen: Those are good starting points — Connor will try to target those in the sim. 
[12:03] Priya Mehta: Any timeline on when we'll get the results? 
[12:07] Connor Patel: If you share traces by Monday, I can run a full replay and get back results within 5 business days. 
[12:14] Liam O'Connor: We'll aim to share them by end of day Monday. 
[12:18] Maya Chen: Great. A couple of notes — we'll include a simple decision tree in the proposal: fully dedicated for regulated tenants, hybrid for general customers, and fallback policies. 
[12:29] Sara Kim: For compliance docs — please include SOC2, SSO guide, and KMS integration steps. 
[12:34] Maya Chen: Will do. 
[12:37] Connor Patel: One technical aside — if you have a custom model fork, we can onboard it but need compatibility checks (KV cache format, tokenizer). That can be part of the pilot. 
[12:47] Priya Mehta: We do have a couple of fine-tuned variants. We'll flag them in the trace file. 
[12:52] Diego Ramos: Are there any network egress costs we should expect with hosted fallback? 
[12:56] Connor Patel: There could be additional egress depending on routing; we'll highlight those in the cost model. 
[13:03] Liam O'Connor: Ok, process question — who signs the security addendum? 
[13:07] Maya Chen: Typically your legal or procurement signs the SDA; we'll include the doc in the proposal for review. 
[13:13] Priya Mehta: One more operational: can we throttle low-priority tenants during spikes automatically? 
[13:18] Connor Patel: Yes, priority-based throttling is supported. You can map tenant priority to fallback order and quota consumption. 
[13:26] Sara Kim: Let's confirm follow-ups: 1) Maya to send proposal and compliance docs, 2) Connor to request traces and run sim, 3) StratoEdge to share traces and p95 targets. 
[13:37] Maya Chen: Correct. I'll also include a suggested pilot timeline. 
[13:41] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. Anything else? 
[13:44] Priya Mehta: Could you also include guidance on model quantization vs quality tradeoffs? A short table would help. 
[13:49] Connor Patel: Sure — we'll include a quantization impact table for your prompt set. 
[13:54] Maya Chen: All right, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and proposed pilot dates. 
[13:59] Liam O'Connor: Great, appreciate the time. 
[14:03] Priya Mehta: Thanks. 
[14:05] Diego Ramos: Bye.
[14:07] End of recording.

Note: Transcription imperfect in places — e.g., "KV cash" appears once in the transcription where speaker meant KV cache; some product names may be transcribed slightly off.
